column4: The section’s n-ṣ-b root (ن ص ب) names fatigue, and its hungry worker receives only exhaustion; this verse says fatigue, thirst, and hunger endured in God’s way are recorded as righteous work and their reward is not lost.
The section says the final account counts deeds; this verse says every small or great expenditure and every valley crossed is recorded so God may reward the best of their work.
The section asks what effort earns and describes a share of work; this verse condemns those who shortchange others, introducing a reversal of fair return.
The section treats effort and its due share; this verse says the defrauders demand full measure when they take from people.
The section’s laborer expects a return; this verse says the defrauders give others less when measuring or weighing for them, the unjust opposite of a fair recompense.
The section ends with God’s account; this verse says God set up the balance, giving a concrete image of measured judgment.
The section describes deeds being counted; this verse commands that the balance not be transgressed, adding the demand for a just measure.
The section contrasts effort that yields satisfaction with effort that fails; this verse requires weighing with justice and forbids giving short measure.
The section’s account counts things and the worker expects a due return; this verse commands full measure and a straight balance, making fairness in allotment concrete.
The section’s final reckoning is exact; this verse commands full measure and just weight and forbids burdening a soul beyond its capacity.
The section’s worker fears effort yielding only fatigue; this verse says God does not wrong even an atom’s weight and multiplies good, assuring exact justice in the return.
The section says each person’s account belongs to God; this verse warns of the return to Him and full payment for what each soul earned without injustice.
The section joins work with a final account; this verse describes gathering for a day when each soul is paid in full for what it earned.
The section’s saʿy gloss includes work and earning; this verse says each soul has what it earned and bears what it acquired, linking deeds to their own account.
The section distinguishes effort by its result; this verse says good work benefits its doer and evil work returns against its doer, while God wrongs no servant.
The section makes effort and its return visible at the account; this verse says a person will be told what they sent ahead and left behind.
The section says one face looks at its effort and is satisfied; this verse makes the person a witness against their own deeds.
The section’s account exposes what effort produced; this neighboring verse completes the self-witness scene by saying excuses will not conceal it.
The section contrasts efforts by whether they stand at the account; this verse identifies people who did not expect any reckoning, a stance that precedes their failed outcome.
The section ends with the account of people’s deeds; this verse introduces guardians appointed over them, setting up the recorders named next.
The section’s account counts what people did; this neighboring verse identifies the appointed guardians as noble recorders.
The section’s ḥisāb (حساب) is counting things; this verse says the recorders know what people do, the specific content of that account.

The section says empty speech is absent from the garden and that account belongs to God; this verse introduces two receivers seated on either side before the next verse says every utterance is watched.
The section ends with God’s account; this verse says hearing, sight, and skin testify against people about what they did.
The section’s account makes deeds answerable; this neighboring verse explains how the skins testify, saying God enabled them to speak.
The section treats even empty excess as omitted from a count; this verse says God can bring a deed to light even if it is a mustard seed hidden in a rock or in the heavens or earth.
The section contrasts temporary exhaustion with a lasting return for worthy effort; this verse says what people have runs out while what is with God remains, and the patient receive their wage.
The section’s saʿy is effort directed toward a result; this verse tells people to race toward forgiveness and a garden, making striving for the lasting reward explicit.
The section connects effort with a garden and final satisfaction; this verse urges hastening to forgiveness and the Garden prepared for the God-conscious.
The section’s source gloss says saʿy can be any good or evil work; this verse tells people to race toward good deeds.
The section joins work to the final account; this verse says whoever hopes to meet the Lord should do righteous work, directly linking effort with that meeting.
The section describes saʿy as effort; this verse says those who strive for God are guided by Him and are with the good-doers.
The section weighs effort by what it yields; this verse says life and death were made to test who is best in deed.
The section says effort will be seen at the final account; this verse commands people to act and says God, His Messenger, and the believers will see their work.
The section links effort to a return; this verse says no soul knows the hidden comfort prepared as a reward for what people did.
The section’s satisfied effort ends in a garden; this verse tells its people they inherit the Garden for what they used to do.
The section’s successful worker is satisfied in a garden; this verse promises lofty chambers in the Garden to those who believe and do good work.
The section links a good return to effort; this neighboring verse identifies patient endurance and trust in the Lord as the qualities of those receiving the promised chambers.
The section defines ḥ-s-b as counting things; this verse promises the patient their wage without account, using account to mark a reward beyond measure.
The section contrasts food that cannot satisfy hunger with the garden reward; this verse gives the righteous a sealed drink of pure nectar.
The section names saʿy as earning work; this verse says the seal is musk and calls competitors to compete for that reward.
The section’s garden reward answers failed sustenance; this neighboring verse says the pure drink is mixed with Tasnīm.
The section contrasts an unsatisfying meal with garden provision; this verse completes the drink scene by identifying Tasnīm as a spring from which those brought near drink.
The section asks what effort will earn at the final account; this verse says wages are paid in full on Resurrection and names escape from the Fire and entry into the Garden as success.
The section’s hungry laborer gets no satisfying return; this verse pictures a thirsty person pursuing a mirage and finding nothing, then meeting God’s full account.
The section contrasts effort that bears reward with effort that fails; this verse compares the deeds of disbelievers to ashes scattered by wind, unable to benefit them.
The section’s root gh-n-y (غ ن ي) concerns sufficiency and what does not avail; this verse says a person’s wealth and earnings will not avail him, joining failed sufficiency directly to earned means.
The section’s n-ṣ-b root (ن ص ب) names fatigue; Moses’ companion uses that same root for weariness from their journey, a concrete bodily-fatigue scene though this verse does not weigh its reward.
The section says effort is counted in the final return; this verse assigns people degrees according to what they did and says God is not unaware of their work.
The section’s dictionary form nasīb (نصيب) means a share; this verse says a person who makes a good or bad intercession receives a share of its consequence.
The section’s share gloss is an allotted portion; this verse describes a known right in the wealth of the righteous, a portion set aside for others.
The section develops the idea of an allotted share; this neighboring verse names the asker and deprived as recipients of the known right in 70:24.

The section contrasts those whose effort earns a garden with those left hungry; this verse names the adverse person’s failure to urge feeding the poor, a concrete neglected deed before the punishment meal.

The section’s root gh-n-y (غ ن ي) concerns what does not suffice; this verse says wealth and children cannot avail those who disbelieve against God’s judgment, a distinct failure of worldly sufficiency.
The section depicts effort that can go astray and fail to return; this verse says the deeds of those who disbelieve and turn others from God’s way are made to stray.
The section says some effort returns only as fatigue; this verse says showy spending is like dust on a smooth rock, washed away so the giver has nothing left.
The section links satisfaction with one’s effort and approval from God; this verse portrays spending for God’s approval as a garden that produces its yield, the fruitful counterpart to 2:264.
The section contrasts empty speech with accounted effort; this verse says good words rise to God and righteous work lifts them, connecting speech to valued action.
The section’s satisfied worker receives a fitting return; this verse states the principle that the reward of good is good.
